title: Toe Drag Release
description: Toe drag to release into a powerful shot. Build up to it.
whatYouNeed: A cone (or puck, bucket, chair with a stick)
dos: Hips rotate toward net, feet stay mostly planted
Start easy, feet not too close to the cone
Drag the puck with the toe, get a powerful pop off release
Elbow up, allow the sling push-pull motion
As you improve, move your feet closer to the cone — release the puck between your feet with weight on top of the puck for flex and power
donts: Don't step away from the cone before the release
Don't look down at the puck the whole time

title: Explosive Pop Snap
description: Train a quicker, more explosive snap that transfers to every shot type.
whatYouNeed: Two broken sticks, 1-3 feet gap between them
dos: Focus solely on the snap
Keep your body relaxed
Pop the puck from the toe of the blade as quick as you can
donts: Don't drag the puck and turn it into a Bedard style shot
You should solely be focusing on the snap release
Don't need to move your feet — body should stay relaxed
notes: Work on this — you should be able to eventually get power on the shot even in this small surface area. Don't worry if it's lighter at first, keep working!

title: Catch & Release Shot
description: Game-like catch and release shot. Train receiving a pass and getting the shot off quickly with your head up — simulates in-game timing.
whatYouNeed: A passer (or a helper), a pile of pucks, a net
dos: Receive the puck and get the shot off quickly
Pick a spot, hit it a few times before switching targets
Keep your head up — scan the net before the shot comes off
Lefties: go low blocker. Righties: go low glove
Build the habit of seeing what the goalie is giving you
donts: Don't look down for a long time — eyes should be scanning the net before you release

title: High Slot One-Timer
description: High slot one-timer drill. Train reading the pass, picking your spot, and snapping it off quick from the slot — simulates the most dangerous scoring area on the ice.
whatYouNeed: A passer (or helper), a pile of pucks, a net
dos: Lefties: shoot top right (right side of net) — where the goalie is sliding toward
Righties: shoot top left (opposite corner)
On a slow pass, go across the grain
Hit five in one spot before moving to the next target
Snap it quick — high slot windows close fast
donts: Don't raise your stick above your head like a slap shot
This is a high slot one-timer, not a blue line bomb — keep the stick lower and snap through the puck

title: Finding Shooting Lanes
description: Change the angle, find the lane. Use a Bedard-style release and forehand-backhand fakes to create space and open up scoring areas.
whatYouNeed: A cone (or bucket/chair), a net, pucks
dos: Let your body flow naturally — be involved in the fake before the shot
Be intentional about where you aim — shoot for practical scoring areas
Remember spots on the net where you've scored in games — aim for those areas
donts: Don't just step to the side and shoot — the Bedard pull needs to bring the puck toward your feet
Don't make the fake with just your stick — use your whole body

title: In Tight Finishing
description: In tight finishing drill. Quick feet, soft hands, one-touch chip shots around the net — everything happens fast in tight.
dos: Keep feet planted, facing the net
Quick dribble stickhandle with body movement on the fake
Focus on chipping the puck up high
Make it a one-touch chip shot — quick and soft
donts: Don't move your feet
Don't do a long wrist shot
Don't fully rotate your body and do a slow long backhander

title: Snapshots on Passer
description: Snapshot off the top of the passer in a limited surface area. Trains you to generate power off the end of your release, building a quicker, more compact snap that's less predictable and highly effective in close quarters. The power transfers to every other shot — even when you're further out and drag the puck for a windup, you still snap and pop at the end.
whatYouNeed: A passer (or helper), a net, pucks
dos: Keep your top hand up high near your chest
Let your hand punch out slightly, then snap back quickly — that's where the pop and spin comes from
Keep your feet still, body relaxed
Watch the demonstration closely and mirror the mechanics
donts: Don't drag the puck into a toe drag release — this drill is pure snap, no angle change needed
Don't stare down at the puck the whole time
Don't pull your stick back and slap at the puck
Don't stress if you're not getting power at first — this takes time to master and pays off long-term for your release
notes: The second video is a slowed-down version without gloves so you can observe the hand mechanics more closely. Both videos show the same drill.

title: Foundation Snap Shot
description: The perfect drill for dialing in your snap shot and correcting form. If your mechanics are off, you won't be able to get power on this shot — the drill forces you to place the puck in the right position and take a compact, proper snap. Great for developing players learning to generate power and confidence in their release. The drill exaggerates the push-puck-away-then-pop technique that's essential to every snap shot.
dos: Drag the puck to a spot where you can one-touch it
Let your hips and body rotate toward the net
Use a staggered stance — copy the footwork shown in the video
Focus specifically on being compact and efficient with every movement
donts: Don't try to overpower it — if your form is off, the shot won't work, so let the drill correct your mechanics
Don't reach for the puck — bring it into your body before releasing
Don't rush the push-pop sequence — it should be one fluid motion
notes: Kids and developing players benefit most from this. The push-puck-away technique gets exaggerated naturally, which is exactly what builds a proper snap shot foundation.
